analysis.one_liner: Writes abortion and contraception rights from past Supreme Court rulings into federal law.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision ended constitutional protection for abortion, this bill would have made the core holdings of Roe v. Wade, Casey, and earlier contraception cases binding federal statute. It would bar states from banning contraception or imposing an "undue burden" on abortion before fetal viability, while still allowing states to restrict abortion after viability and to pass health and safety rules. Individuals and the Justice Department could sue to stop state laws that violate it.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and people who need contraception or abortion services, especially in states that have banned or heavily restricted abortion since the Dobbs ruling. The bill would restore a nationwide right to abortion before fetal viability, protect access to contraception against state bans, allow abortion after viability when the woman's life or health is at risk, and give individuals or the Justice Department the power to sue states that violate these rights, with attorney's fees available. Abortion providers and clinics would also regain a stable legal foundation nationwide.

how_it_helps.text: It writes the core holdings of Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey into federal statute, restoring a nationwide right to abortion before fetal viability after the Supreme Court removed constitutional protection in Dobbs.
It bars states from prohibiting individuals from obtaining or using contraceptives, protecting access to birth control.

It preserves exceptions allowing abortion after viability when the pregnant woman's life or health is at risk, and lets the Justice Department or any affected person sue in federal or state court to block violating state laws, with attorney's fees available to prevailing parties.

analysis.who_pays: State governments that have banned or restricted abortion would lose the ability to enforce those laws, and anti-abortion organizations that litigate in support of state restrictions would face suits challenging them. Taxpayers would bear the cost of federal enforcement through the Justice Department.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows abortion before fetal viability with only health and safety regulations, which opponents view as permitting abortion throughout most of pregnancy and overriding the state bans many voters have chosen.

Its constitutionality is uncertain: after Dobbs held that abortion is not constitutionally protected, opponents argue Congress lacks power to override state laws on this subject, even under its Fourteenth Amendment and commerce authority.
The 'undue burden' standard invites years of litigation over which state regulations survive, and conscience protections for objecting providers are preserved only by a rule of construction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore nationwide protections for contraception and pre-viability abortion with narrow post-viability exceptions, at the cost of overriding state bans. Its main design risks are that it could be challenged as beyond Congress's power after Dobbs and that it leaves room for litigation over what counts as an "undue burden," but its framework deliberately mirrors the Casey rules that governed for nearly thirty years. Because it never received any committee action, the costs were never tested on the record; the practical result is simply that no federal protection exists.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2023 and, on the same day, read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action of any kind is listed in the action history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.
Because the bill died, the Dobbs decision remained controlling law, and state legislatures continued to set abortion policy without any federal statutory floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's outcome leaves in place the state-by-state abortion rules that followed the Dobbs decision, so state legislatures that restricted abortion and the organized movements that backed them are better off; women in ban states continue to bear the cost of traveling for care.

for.name: Sens. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and Kyrsten Sinema

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor and, as the majority in committee scheduling, no Judiciary action occurred

against.name: Anti-abortion organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal abortion-rights legislation and lobbied against it

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was mostly Democratic with notable Republican and Independent support, but there is no vote record to measure the partisan split because it never left committee.

industries.industry: Abortion providers and women's health clinics
industries.note: The bill would restore a nationwide legal foundation for pre-viability abortion services, reversing the patchwork of state bans that forced many clinics to close. For patients, it would mean access to care closer to home rather than interstate travel.

industries.industry: Crisis pregnancy centers and anti-abortion organizations
industries.note: State restrictions these groups support could be challenged in federal court as undue burdens, and their litigation costs could rise under the attorney's fee provision.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical and contraceptive supply chains operating under state bans
industries.note: States could no longer prohibit obtaining or using contraceptives, removing legal uncertainty for manufacturers and distributors of contraception in restrictive states.
